title: Enterprise Cryptographic Discovery & Analysis Tool (ECDAT)
dataset_link: Standard Open source datasets for source code repositories (eg:Github), libraries (eg: Openssl) may be used.
description:
• Background Transitioning to Post Quantum Cryptography based solutions requires preparedness, risk assessment and financial and operational investment. Towards this, discovery and inventory of Cryptographic Artefacts is the critical first step, that will enable the transition.
• Description i. Identify and catalogue all cryptographic artefacts (algorithms, keys, certificates, protocols, libraries, hardware modules, cloud services) across internal and external facing applications, products and infrastructure.
ii. The tool should perform a comprehensive quantum risk assessment and identify systems prone to potential quantum attacks, and highlight risks to sensitive data.
iii. Classify all the artefacts by type, lifetime and business criticality. Apply structured frameworks such as Mosca’s algorithm (compare data lifetime plus migration time against expected arrival of cryptographic relevant quantum computer) to identify and categorize risks.
iv. Recommend suitable alternatives (PQC/ Hybrid algorithms) for applications based on risk profile, latency, cost, etc.
• Expected Solution/Deliverables:
A Comprehensive CBOM analytics tool that can scan Source code repositories, binaries, libraries and container images, for assessing risks (due to quantum computers), classifying artefacts and suggesting alternatives: - Produce a report displaying all cryptographic assets including versions/ modes in standardised formats Interactive GUI platform to visualise the scan, risks and results
summary: Innovation (3/5): draws on quantum applied to a blockchain & cybersecurity problem, placing it in the moderate band. Feasibility (4/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a working prototype is realistic in a 36-hour window. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Blockchain & Cybersecurity. Tech Depth (4/5): centers on algorithm, infrastructure. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (3/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 19/30 -> Yellow verdict.

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a tool that scans an organization's code, binaries, and infrastructure to find and catalog every cryptographic algorithm, key, and certificate in use, then flags which ones are vulnerable to future quantum computers and recommends safer alternatives.
overview.why_it_matters: Organizations can't plan their transition to quantum-resistant cryptography without first knowing what cryptography they're actually using. This inventory step is the genuine, necessary first move toward quantum readiness.
pain_points: Organizations lack a comprehensive inventory of their cryptographic artefacts across applications and infrastructure.
No systematic way to assess quantum-computing risk across an existing cryptographic estate.
Migration planning to post-quantum cryptography needs risk-prioritized guidance, not just a raw inventory list.
overview.background: Transitioning to post-quantum cryptography requires first discovering and cataloging existing cryptographic artefacts across an organization, then assessing quantum risk using frameworks like Mosca's algorithm.
overview.whats_being_asked: A Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) analytics tool scanning source code, binaries, libraries for cryptographic artefacts, performing quantum risk assessment (Mosca's algorithm), and recommending PQC/hybrid alternatives.
expected_solution: Cryptographic artefact discovery across source code, binaries, libraries.
Classification by type, lifetime, and business criticality.
Quantum risk assessment using structured frameworks (Mosca's algorithm).

analysis.innovation_scope_note: High. Genuine cryptographic artefact discovery across code/binaries plus quantum-risk-framework application is real, technically substantial, and genuinely timely given the post-quantum transition.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Moderate-high. Static analysis for cryptographic pattern detection is achievable using established techniques; genuine Mosca's-algorithm-based risk framing is real, specialized applied cryptography knowledge.

competitive_landscape.note: Requires genuine cryptography and static-analysis expertise together, a specialized, narrow field, though commercial CBOM tools exist as reference points.

innovation.note: Genuine CBOM discovery plus quantum-risk-framework application is real, technically substantial, and timely work.

invention.note: Static analysis for cryptographic pattern detection uses established techniques; genuine Mosca's algorithm application is real specialized depth.

technical_feasibility.note: Full coverage across all named artefact types (algorithms, keys, certs, protocols, libraries, hardware, cloud) isn't achievable in 36 hours, scope to source-code/library scanning as your core.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly supports genuine, currently-urgent organizational post-quantum migration planning.

architecture.note: Static-analysis scanning plus a risk-classification/recommendation layer, well-understood pattern applied to a genuinely valuable, timely problem.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick, genuinely achievable when scoped to source-code/library scanning (the most tractable artefact type) rather than claiming full coverage across binaries, hardware modules, and cloud services in 36 hours.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Genuinely timely, real organizational need given active post-quantum cryptography transition pressure across industry.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Attempting comprehensive coverage across all named artefact types (source, binaries, libraries, hardware modules, cloud services) in 36 hours is unrealistic, scope to source-code/library scanning as your credible core.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Scope your discovery engine to source-code and library scanning (using established cryptographic API/pattern detection), and apply Mosca's algorithm genuinely and correctly to at least a representative sample of discovered artefacts, rather than attempting comprehensive infrastructure-wide discovery.

idea_0_4: Research Mosca's algorithm and real cryptographic pattern-detection approaches for source code/library scanning.
Choose a sample codebase (your own test repository with various cryptographic library usage) to scan.
Split: one person on the discovery/scanning engine, one on the risk-classification and recommendation logic.
prototype_4_22: Build your cryptographic artefact discovery engine scanning source code/libraries for known cryptographic API usage patterns.
Build classification logic by algorithm type and estimated business criticality.
Start Mosca's algorithm-based quantum risk assessment logic.
integration_22_30: Connect discovery, classification, and risk assessment into one coherent pipeline.
Test against your sample codebase with deliberately varied cryptographic usage (strong modern algorithms, known-weak/legacy algorithms).
Build PQC/hybrid algorithm recommendation logic based on risk assessment.
polish_30_36: Build a clear CBOM report output with risk-prioritized findings and recommendations.
Rehearse presenting your Mosca's algorithm application and how it correctly prioritized your test cases.
Prepare to discuss your scoping choice (source/library scanning) versus the full multi-artefact-type vision.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show your tool correctly discovering and risk-classifying cryptographic usage in your test codebase, with a clear, correctly-applied Mosca's algorithm calculation for at least one artefact (comparing data lifetime plus migration time against quantum threat timeline), and a sensible PQC/hybrid recommendation, that genuine, correct application of the named framework is the real technical substance here.

strengths: Genuinely timely, real organizational need given active post-quantum transition pressure.
Established techniques exist for cryptographic pattern detection in source code.
weaknesses: Full coverage across all named artefact types isn't achievable in 36 hours, requires honest scoping.
Genuine, correct application of Mosca's algorithm needs real understanding of the framework, not superficial labeling.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Don't skip real research into Mosca's algorithm, applying it correctly is a specific, checkable requirement in this PS.
team_fit.approach: Scope to source-code/library scanning as your reliable core before considering any broader artefact-type coverage.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard static-analysis pattern-matching scaffolding for known cryptographic library APIs.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Correctly understanding and applying Mosca's algorithm (comparing data security lifetime plus migration time against estimated quantum threat timeline), that requires real applied cryptography domain knowledge.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-scaffolded tool that labels findings as 'quantum risk' without genuinely applying Mosca's algorithm's actual timeline-comparison logic would misrepresent the analytical rigor this PS specifically asks for.

data_resource_availability.status: No external dataset dependency, your own or a public sample codebase with varied cryptographic library usage is sufficient for testing.

judge_qna.question: How does your tool actually apply Mosca's algorithm, not just label something as 'quantum risk'?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Walk through your specific calculation for a discovered artefact, data security lifetime plus estimated migration time compared against the estimated timeline for cryptographically-relevant quantum computers, showing the actual comparison logic.
judge_qna.follow_up: What assumptions did you make about quantum computer timeline estimates, and how sensitive is your risk classification to that assumption?

judge_qna.question: Why did you scope to source-code scanning instead of the full range of artefact types named (binaries, hardware, cloud)?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be direct that comprehensive coverage isn't achievable in 36 hours, and source/library scanning demonstrates the core discovery-and-risk-assessment logic that would extend to other artefact types with additional engineering.
judge_qna.follow_up: What would change technically when extending to binary analysis versus source-code analysis?
